rv.q: Watching these two angry, broken, world-weary animals circle each other is an uncomfortable pleasure.
Too bad the writing isn’t sufficiently nuanced to make her calvary more affecting.
Whether you prefer the foghorn drawl of Ms. Turner or the more soothing tones of Dr. Drew, of “Celebrity Rehab” fame, is essentially just a matter of taste.
Now if we could only get Turner back onstage in a role worthy of her.
Turner does her best to bring warmth and intelligence to the brass-knuckled nun, but this troubled saint remains a flimsy character in a hollow play.

As the show's bathos emissions rise and rise to thyroid-killing levels...[the show] would be in a church basement or the sanctuary of some some mega-tabernacle. Which is where High, minus a few dozen of Turner's f-bombs and all references to sodomy, might be heading soon, too, and maybe where it was meant to be all along.
But if you grew up watching Bugs Bunny and "The Wizard of Oz" instead of Nickelodeon and "High School Musical," then you'll likely find "Wonderland" to be too namby-pamby for words.
Turner brings her patented husky swagger to the main role, but to little effect; she’s mother superior to a thin weepie that’s quite inferior.
It's shameful that High never manages to dig any deeper in that moment or any moment.
Alas, for the most part, High gave me a crisis of my own.
Rob Ruggiero's obvious direction does little to mask the writing's flaws, nor do the actors transcend them.
Nevertheless, the play comes off as a dull three-character mystery that pales in comparison with more compelling thrillers such as "Equus" and "Agnes of God."
Lombardo, a recovering addict, has written an imitation of a play, and not a very good one.
Despite its manipulative aspects, the play is nonetheless reasonably compelling due to the inherent emotional power of its subject matter.
